title: US credit-card banking combines broad household use with unusually high lending spreads and returns
source_unit: US credit-card monthly account, issuer economics, and lending-return measures

observations.period: Regulatory account-level data; monthly accounts and current credit-card market

denominator.unit: monthly US credit-card accounts; approximately 90% of the US credit-card market

spread_over_short_rate.unit: percentage points over the short rate

household_borrower_share.unit: approximately percent of households that are credit-card borrowers

observations.method: NBER working paper analysis of regulatory account-level data and lifetime cash flows across 550 million monthly accounts.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract reports rounded market averages and an approximate household-borrower share; account coverage is very broad but is not a linked household panel of income, repayment burden, product choice, or welfare.
observations.subgroup: US credit-card accounts and households using credit cards; account-level measures are not interchangeable with household-level outcomes.
observations.counterinterpretation: A high rate or spread can reflect default risk, rewards, operating costs, credit access, and product selection; it does not by itself establish excessive pricing or realized household harm.

observations.period: Regulatory account-level data; credit-card lending economics

denominator.unit: monthly US credit-card accounts in the study's approximately 90% market-coverage sample

return_on_assets_after_expenses.unit: percent return on assets after operating and other expenses

banking_sector_roa_multiple.unit: approximately multiple of the banking sector return on assets

default_risk_premium.unit: percent default risk premium priced into credit-card rates

credit_card_lending_alpha.unit: percent alpha relative to the aggregate bank sector after accounting for default risk

observations.method: Lifetime cash-flow accounting and cross-sectional estimation using regulatory account-level data.
observations.uncertainty: The reported ROA, risk-premium, and alpha estimates depend on the paper's accounting definitions, risk adjustment, sample coverage, and model assumptions; they are lender-side estimates rather than consumer-welfare estimates.
observations.subgroup: Credit-card lending portfolios and aggregate bank-sector comparison.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher returns may compensate for servicing, marketing, fraud, liquidity, and default risks not captured by a simple rate comparison; profitability does not identify how competition, regulation, or borrower alternatives would change outcomes.

related_sources.claim: US merchant-level comparator estimating payment-system redistribution through interchange fees and rewards.
Official market, balance, APR, fee, promotional-product, and dispute context.

boundary: This record establishes a broad US credit-card account and lender-economics layer. It does not establish the same household's APR, repayment burden, approval or denial, reward net benefit, merchant-price incidence, causal market power, or successful remedy. The account, lender, merchant, and household units remain separate.
